newsitem.title: INDIA: Strike cripples India state after leader's arrest.
newsitem.headline: Strike cripples India state after leader's arrest.

text.p: Activists barricaded roads and clashed with baton-wielding policemen in India's second most populous state on Friday as the ruling party led a general strike to protest against its leader's arrest in a corruption scandal.

An estimated 5,000 paramilitary men joined to help police at sensitive points in the eastern Bihar state, but there were no major violent incidents during the strike that brought business to a standstill, officials and witnesses said.
Police said 10 people, including a federal lawmaker, were injured at Patna, the state capital, when members of the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) party clashed with baton-wielding police.

"Ten people were injured. It happened during a demonstration," a police official told Reuters at a busy square in the city's business district, where shops and offices were shut while slogan-shouting activists roamed around.

Laloo Prasad Yadav, a charismatic leader of the lower castes, began a two-week remand on Wednesday after surrendering to a court in the $280-million "fodder scam" in which federal police have filed corruption charges that the leader vehemently denies.

Yadav, first indicted in April, resigned as Bihar's chief minister a week ago after a court issued an arrest warrant. He failed in his attempts to win "anticipatory bail" to avoid arrest in the scandal involving suspected misuse of animal welfare funds.
Stick-wielding activists forced shops to close, erected barriers with uprooted lamp-posts and chained bicycle rickshaws across roads. Women protestors formed a chain by holding hands.
"Police did not do much," said Amarendra Kumar Amar, an RJD activist.
Witnesses reported isolated incidents of stone-throwing which damaged the windshields of passing cars.

RJD activists, some of them wearing the party's green head bands and holding up portraits of their leader, shouted slogans alleging discrimination in corruption cases, saying upper caste leaders like former Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao had been granted bail while low-caste leader Yadav had not.
"Why bail for forwards, why jail for backwards," they said.
Hindu caste animosities and tussles between landlords and peasants often spell violence in the poor state of 93 million people, of whom 61 percent cannot read or write.
"We are closing down everything. We will not stop until he is released," said Vijaya Singh, an RJD leader.
Activists plan to launch on Saturday a "fill the jails" campaign, offering themselves collectively for arrest.
Yadav named his unschooled wife, Rabri Devi, as chief minister in a move that sparked protests from the opposition. Devi, a 38-year-old mother of nine children, led the strike on Friday.
Politicians say Devi must ensure peace to defuse the opposition demands that she be relieved of office.
"Police and magistrates have been deployed all over the state at all sensitive points," Chief Secretary B.P. Varma, the state's top civil servant, said earlier on Friday.

India's ruling 15-party United Front coalition has been sharply divided by a debate over corruption and Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral has faced criticism over his failure to take firm action against Yadav.
Yadav, who ruled Bihar for seven years, formed his breakaway RJD party last month, alleging irregularities in the leadership elections of Gujral's Janata Dal party, which he had headed until then.
